Consider a linked list given in the figure below.

What is the value of $\textsf{n} \rightarrow \textsf{next}\rightarrow \textsf{next}\rightarrow \textsf{next}\rightarrow \textsf{data}?$

Where $n$ and head are pointers to the following struct type and intitallised as per the figure shown.

struct node{
 int data;
 struct node *next;
};
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)

Answer: C

n -> next-> next-> next-> data;

n is the pointer to node containing the value 40.

n → next → next → next is the pointer to node containing the value 30.

node(30) → data = 30.

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

Answer: Option C 30

In the given linked list there are two pointers: head and n.

head points to the node with a data value of 10, and n points to the node with a data value of 40.

now in the question it is asking n→ next→ next→ next→ data

let’s break down the question,

In step 1:- n $=$ n → next // at this step n will point to where the head is pointing as it is a circular singly linked list i.e. at 10.

step 2:- n $=$ n → next // at this step n will point to the node containing data value as 20.

step 3:- n $=$ n → next // at this step n will point to the node containing data value as 30

so in the above three steps, all three next operations have been done

step 4:- n → data since n is pointing to the node which contains data 30 so n → data =30.

Consider a function ReverseList() which has following protype -

Node *ReverseList(Node *p)

Function reverse the nodes in a given linked list.

That is, head = ReverseList(head); will take a list held by head, reverse it and put back to head.

Node * ReverseList(Node * p) {
 if (!p) return NULL;
 if (p -> next) {
 Node * q = ReverseList(p -> next);
 p -> next -> next = p;
 p -> next = 0;
 return ______; //Line X
 }
 return ______; //Line Y
}


Fill in the blanks for Line X and Line Y. If we say Line X is filled by $p$ then we consider Line X as $\textbf{return p;}$ after filling the blank.
Line X and Line Y should be filled by which values respectively such that the function correctly reverses the given linked list.
questions.solution:
Answer: D

Selected solution (score: 5)

This is bit lengthy explanation, Please bear with me till end.

Before everything draw recursive calls and see where $p, p \rightarrow n, q $ is pointing.
Let’s start by understanding the function. Let SLL be $1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow Null$
In if condition there are line 1,2,3,X.

We will go inside if loop only if $p \rightarrow n$ is not null i.e. is pointing $3$ in $3 \rightarrow 4\rightarrow Null$.
In last recursive call p will be pointing last node i.e. 3 and if condition is false, line Y will be executed first.
Here we have 3 options to return at line Y:

  1. p
  2. $p \rightarrow n$, which is Null
  3. q

Notice that we are not going in if loop so local var q is not created. for sake of understanding, Lets take q as Null and use it instead of 2nd option.

lets analyze line (2,3)
suppose the p is pointing to 2 in LL $2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow Null$
after line (2,3), Node 3 will point to Node 2 and Node 2 will point to Null. i.e. $3 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow Null$ Note that p is still pointing to 2.

At the end of recursion we saw line Y can return q(Null) or p which is being assigned to q.
q is not being modified here and so in line X if we return q, then Null will be returned throughout the calls and sent to head. Which will not be peaceful :) So, line Y can only return p.

Now about line X, our objective is $1 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow Null$ to $3 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 1 \rightarrow Null$.
Draw recursion call, See that in second last recursive call q has address of Node 3 and p is pointing to Node 2.
now as per analysis of line (2,3), it will manipulate pointer, now comes line X. Again Two choices :

  1. if we return p, it will be assigned to q. However p value is different in each call and last node address will be lost. i.e. if IP $6 \rightarrow 7 \rightarrow 8$ then OP $6$.
  2. if we return q then we have last node address in q and as mentioned earlier q is not being modified hence we will return it to head and we will have reversed list.
Source solution 2 (score: 8)

We can also think by eliminating the options and then checking what will reverse the list.

options A and B can be eliminated like this :

think of minimal case when list has one element, in that case the head should point to the single element only just like original list. A → NULL ( p points to A )

so since p->next = NULL in this case, we won’t enter the if block . It is obvious that now line Y should return p only ( because in case of single element the list remains unchanged. )

Now consider options C and D :

again think of a small list of 2 elements :

suppose A → B→ NULL

here we enter if block as p → next is not NULL and q will point to B only as we recursively call reverselist( p->next ) and inside that B → next is NULL so pointer to B is returned ( it is the same case of single element list as above )

now after two lines of pointer manipulation , list will be : NULL ← A ← B

it is mentioned in the question we return a pointer to head of the list after reversing it so, pointer to B is returned which is actually q only . ( q –> next that is A is not the head after reversing )

therefore, option D is correct.

Source solution 3 (score: 2)

Based on the recursive logic for reversing a linked list, let's analyze the code step-by-step to fill in the blanks.

1. Understanding the Base Case (Line Y)

  • The function first checks if (!p) return NULL;.

  • Then it enters the if (p -> next) block only if there is a next node.

  • If p -> next is NULL (meaning p is the last node of the list), the if block is skipped, and execution goes directly to Line Y.

  • When reversing a list, the last node of the original list becomes the head of the reversed list. Therefore, the function must return a pointer to this node.

  • So, Line Y must be p.

2. Understanding the Recursive Step (Line X)

  • Inside the if block, the function calls itself recursively: Node * q = ReverseList(p -> next);.

  • The variable q stores the result of this call. In a correct implementation, the recursive call returns the new head of the reversed sub-list.

  • The lines p -> next -> next = p; and p -> next = 0; perform the actual reversal of the link for the current node p.

  • After reversing the current node's link, the function needs to return the head of the entire reversed list to its caller.

  • The head of the reversed list is the same node that was returned by the recursive call (the original tail of the list). This node is pointed to by q. The node p has simply been attached to the end of the chain headed by q.

  • Therefore, to propagate the new head up the recursion stack, Line X must return q.

Conclusion

  • Line X: return q;

  • Line Y: return p;

Comparing this with the given options:

A. p and p -> next

B. p and q (Incorrect: q is not defined in the scope of Line Y)

C. q -> next and p

D. q and p

The correct match is D.

questions.qtext:
The intent of the function below is to delete the last node of the list.

void removeLast(Node* first) {
 Node *p, *q;
 p = first;
 q = p->next;
 while (q->next != NULL) {
 p = q;
 q = q->next;
 }
 p->next = NULL;
 free(q);
}

Which of the following describes the class of all linked lists for which this function works correctly?

options.text: All linked lists with more than one node
The empty list and all linked lists with more than one node

questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 1)
This code is not Working when we have circular linked list. Then how option c is correct.
Source solution 2 (score: 0)

This program does not handle the cases :

  1. Where the linked list is empty(doesn’t check if first is NULL or not) thus p = first will give a segmentation fault here.
  2. Only one node. q = q → first gives segmentation fault here.

It works well for other cases i.e. linked list having more than one node. So, (C) is the correct option.

Source solution 3 (score: 0)

Based on a step-by-step analysis of the code with different types of linked lists, here is the evaluation:

1. Empty List (first is NULL)

  • p = first; sets p to NULL.

  • q = p->next; attempts to access memory at NULL->next.

  • Result: This will cause a Segmentation Fault (crash). So, it fails for empty lists.

2. List with exactly one node (first points to a node, next is NULL)

  • p = first; sets p to the first node.

  • q = p->next; sets q to NULL (since there is only one node).

  • while (q->next != NULL) attempts to access NULL->next.

  • Result: This will also cause a Segmentation Fault (crash). So, it fails for single-node lists.

3. List with two or more nodes

  • p points to the first node.

  • q points to the second node (which is not NULL).

  • Loop logic: The while loop correctly traverses the list until q points to the last node and p points to the second-to-last node.

  • Termination: p->next = NULL correctly breaks the link to the last node, and free(q) correctly deallocates the memory for the last node.

  • Result: The function works correctly.

Conclusion:

The function works correctly only if the list has enough nodes to prevent q from being NULL initially. This requires the list to have at least two nodes.

Therefore, the correct option is:

C. All linked lists with more than one node

questions.qtext: Which of the following statement is/are FALSE? Assume that $\log$ base is $2$ in all options.

options.text: If $f, g$, and $h$ are functions from the natural numbers to the non-negative real numbers with $f(n) \geq g(n) \forall n \geq 1, f(n) \in \Theta(h(n))$, and $g(n) \in \Theta(h(n))$, then $(f(n)-g(n)) \in \Theta(h(n))$
$(\log n)^{a}$ is $\mathrm{O}\left(n^{ b}\right)$ for any constant $a$, and for any constant $b>0$
$T(n) = O(f(n))$ and $g(n)$ is a function whose value is never negative then $g(n) T(n)$ is $O(g(n) f(n))$

questions.solution:
Answer: B

Selected solution (score: 22)

Lets explore each options one by one :-

Option A :- $8^{log(n^{2})}$ $\epsilon$ $\theta (n^{6})$

$8^{log(n^{2})}$ = $(n^{2})^{log8}$

= $(n^{2})^{3}$ = $\theta(n^6)$ $\therefore$ Correct option.

Option B :- Lets take $f(n)=n^{2} + 10$ and $g(n)=n^{2}$ and $h(n)=n^{2}$

then $(f(n) – g(n)) =n^{2}+10-n^{2}$ $\epsilon$ $\theta(1)$

$\therefore$ The given statement $(f(n) – g(n)) $ $\epsilon$ $\theta (h(n))$ does not holds hence inccorect.

Option C :- Any power of $logn$ will always be asymtotially lesser than any power of $n$ because growth of $n^{c} where c>0$ is always greater than than of $logn^{k} where k>=1$ .

Hence the given option is correct.

Option D :- If $g(n)$ is an increasing function and when multiplied with any function then rate of growth will only increase or remain same but never will it decrease.

Given that :- $T(n)=Of(n)$ and $g(n)$ is given to be positive function

Hence $g(n).T(n) =O( g(n)f(n))$ holds so given option is correct.

Source solution 2 (score: 0)

Based on the analysis of each option, the correct answer is B.

Here is the step-by-step explanation for why each statement is true or false.

Option A: $8^{\log(n^2)} \in \Theta(n^6)$ — TRUE

Let's simplify the expression using logarithm rules. The problem states the base is 2.

  1. Simplify the exponent: $\log_2(n^2) = 2 \log_2 n$.

  2. Substitute back: The expression becomes $8^{(2 \log_2 n)}$.

  3. Rewrite the base: We know $8 = 2^3$. So, $(2^3)^{(2 \log_2 n)} = 2^{(6 \log_2 n)}$.

  4. Apply power rule: $2^{(6 \log_2 n)} = (2^{\log_2 n})^6$.

  5. Simplify: Since $2^{\log_2 n} = n$, this simplifies to $n^6$.

Since $n^6$ is exactly $\Theta(n^6)$, this statement is TRUE.

Option B: If $f, g \in \Theta(h(n))$, then $(f(n) - g(n)) \in \Theta(h(n))$ — FALSE

This statement claims that if two functions grow at the same rate, their difference must also grow at that same rate. We can disprove this with a simple counter-example where the leading terms cancel out.

Counter-Example:

  • Let $h(n) = n$.

  • Let $f(n) = n + 10$. Clearly, $f(n) \in \Theta(n)$.

  • Let $g(n) = n$. Clearly, $g(n) \in \Theta(n)$.

  • Also, $f(n) \ge g(n)$ for all $n \ge 1$.

Now, calculate the difference:

$$f(n) - g(n) = (n + 10) - n = 10$$

Is $10 \in \Theta(n)$? No. $10$ is a constant, which is $\Theta(1)$, not linear growth like $n$. The difference grew significantly slower than the original functions.

Because we found a case where the conclusion fails, this statement is FALSE.

Option C: $(\log n)^a$ is $O(n^b)$ for constants $a, b > 0$ — TRUE

This is a fundamental property of asymptotic growth: Polynomials always dominate Polylogarithms.

No matter how huge the power of the log is (e.g., $(\log n)^{1000}$) and how tiny the power of $n$ is (e.g., $n^{0.0001}$), as $n$ goes to infinity, the polynomial $n^b$ will eventually become larger and stay larger.

Mathematically:

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{(\log n)^a}{n^b} = 0$$

Since the limit is 0, $(\log n)^a$ is strictly smaller than $n^b$ for large $n$, which means it is $O(n^b)$. This statement is TRUE.

Option D: If $T(n) = O(f(n))$, then $g(n)T(n) = O(g(n)f(n))$ — TRUE

This follows directly from the definition of Big-O notation and basic algebra.

  1. Premise: $T(n) = O(f(n))$ means there exists a constant $c$ such that $T(n) \le c \cdot f(n)$ for large $n$.

  2. Multiply: Since $g(n)$ is never negative, we can multiply both sides of the inequality by $g(n)$ without flipping the sign:

    $$g(n) \cdot T(n) \le g(n) \cdot [c \cdot f(n)]$$

  3. Rearrange:

    $$g(n)T(n) \le c \cdot [g(n)f(n)]$$

  4. Conclusion: This inequality matches the definition of Big-O for the new terms. Thus, $g(n)T(n) = O(g(n)f(n))$.

This statement is TRUE.

Consider Iterated logarithm of $n$, written log ${ }^{\star} n$. Defined as below.
$$\lg ^{*} N=\min \{k \mid \underbrace{\lg \lg \cdots \lg }_{k} N \leq 1\}$$
Which of the following is TRUE?

(log base can be considered as any constant)

options.text: $\lg \lg { }^{*} n=o\left(\lg ^{*} \lg n\right)$ here o is small oh
$\lg ^{*} \lg n=o\left(\lg \lg ^{*} n\right)$ here $o$ is small oh
$\lg ^{\star} \lg n$ and $\lg \lg ^{\ast} n$ are not comparable

Source solution 1 (score: 23)

now if we compare both $f(N)$ and $g(N)$ we get the relation

$f(N) = o (g(N))$

Hence Option A is the correct answer.

    $log^*n$ is the number of times we need to apply logarithm to make a number $\leq1$

    For example:

    $n = 16$

    $log(16) = 4$,

    $log(4) = 2$,

    $log(2) = 1$, stop

    We applied log 3 times, $log^*(n) = 3$

    For some n, you must apply $log$ k times to make $n \leq 1$

    \[ log^*n = k \]

    \[ log(log^*n) = log(k) \]

    Source solution 6 (score: 0)

    Example using $n = 2^{65536}$ for better understanding what's happening

    First, let's establish $X$ by finding the iterated logarithm of $n$:

    $$n = 2^{65536} \rightarrow 65536 \rightarrow 16 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 1$$

    It takes 5 steps to reach 1, so $X = \lg^ n = 5$*.

    Now, applying the two functions:

    1. $\lg^*(\lg n)$

    • The Logic: This represents the iterated log of the result of the first log step. It is equivalent to $X - 1$.

    • The Math: $\lg n = 65536$.

      $\lg^*(65536)$ takes 4 steps ($16 \rightarrow 4 \rightarrow 2 \rightarrow 1$).

    • Result: $4$

    2. $\lg^*(\lg n)$

    • The Logic: This is just a standard logarithm applied to the value $X$. It is equivalent to $\lg(X)$.

    • The Math: We know $\lg^* n = 5$.

      We simply calculate $\lg(5)$.

    • Result: $\approx$ $2.32$

    Even for a massive number like $2^{65536}$, the difference is distinct:

    • $\lg^*(\lg n) = 4$ (Linear reduction of $X$)

    • $\lg(\lg^* n) \approx 2.32$ (Logarithmic reduction of $X$)


    Hence,

    • $\lg \lg^* n$ is $\lg(\lg^* n)$, or $\lg(X)$.

    • $\lg^* \lg n$ is $\lg^*(\lg n)$, or $X-1$.

    • $\lg(X) = o(X-1)$.

    • $\lg \lg^* n = o(\lg^* \lg n)$

    Hope this Helps!

questions.qtext:
Arrange the following functions in their increasing order of growth.

$\left(\begin{array}{c}
\text { If f(n) = O(g(n) and g(n) = O(h((n)) then order is f(n), g(n), h(n).}
\end{array}\right)$

In all options $\log^{2}n$ means $(\log n)^{2}$
questions.solution:
Answer: C

Source solution 1 (score: 2)

Answer is Option C

Assume log base is 2

We can write $\left ( \sqrt{2} \right )^{logn}= \sqrt{n} ,4^{\log n}=n^{2},2^{\log^{2}n}= n^{\log n}$ ----- (1)

From (1) we can say $5\sqrt{n}= O\left ( \left ( \sqrt{2} \right )^{\log n}\right ) , \left ( \sqrt{2} \right )^{\log n}=O\left ( 4^{logn} \right ),4^{logn}= O\left ( 2^{\log^{2}n} \right )$

Given If f(n) = O(g(n) and g(n) = O(h((n)) then order is f(n), g(n), h(n).

$\therefore 5\sqrt{n},\left ( \sqrt{2} \right )^{\log n},4^{\log n},2^{\log ^{2}n}$ are in increasing order of their growth

Source solution 2 (score: 1)

To determine the correct order, let's analyze the asymptotic growth of each function by simplifying them. We will assume the standard base 2 for the logarithm ($\log_2 n$), which is standard in computer science contexts involving terms like $4^{\log n}$.

Here are the four functions given in the options:

  1. $f_1(n) = 5\sqrt{n}$

  2. $f_2(n) = (\sqrt{2})^{\log n}$

  3. $f_3(n) = 4^{\log n}$

  4. $f_4(n) = 2^{\log^2 n}$

Step 1: Simplify each function

  • Function 1: $5\sqrt{n}$

    This is already simplified. It grows linearly with the square root of $n$.

    • Complexity: $\Theta(\sqrt{n}) = \Theta(n^{0.5})$

  • Function 2: $(\sqrt{2})^{\log n}$

    We can rewrite the base $\sqrt{2}$ as $2^{0.5}$.

    $$(\sqrt{2})^{\log n} = (2^{0.5})^{\log n} = 2^{0.5 \log n}$$

    Using the property $a^{\log n} = n^{\log a}$:

    $$2^{\log (n^{0.5})} = n^{0.5} = \sqrt{n}$$

    • Complexity: $\Theta(\sqrt{n}) = \Theta(n^{0.5})$

  • Function 3: $4^{\log n}$

    We can rewrite the base 4 as $2^2$.

    $$4^{\log n} = (2^2)^{\log n} = 2^{2 \log n}$$

    Using logarithm rules ($2 \log n = \log n^2$):

    $$2^{\log (n^2)} = n^2$$

    • Complexity: $\Theta(n^2)$

  • Function 4: $2^{\log^2 n}$

    Note that $\log^2 n$ means $(\log n) \cdot (\log n)$.

    $$2^{(\log n)(\log n)} = (2^{\log n})^{\log n}$$

    Since $2^{\log n} = n$:

    $$= n^{\log n}$$

    • Complexity: $\Theta(n^{\log n})$

Step 2: Compare the orders of growth

Now we compare the simplified forms:

  1. $\Theta(n^{0.5})$ (from $5\sqrt{n}$ and $(\sqrt{2})^{\log n}$)

  2. $\Theta(n^2)$

  3. $\Theta(n^{\log n})$

Comparison:

  • $n^{0.5}$ is the smallest growth rate.

  • $n^2$ grows faster than $n^{0.5}$ but is a polynomial with a fixed exponent.

  • $n^{\log n}$ grows the fastest because the exponent $\log n$ increases as $n$ increases. For any $n > 4$, $\log n > 2$, making $n^{\log n}$ larger than $n^2$. This is sometimes called "super-polynomial" or "quasi-polynomial" growth.

The Hierarchy:

$$\Theta(\sqrt{n}) < \Theta(n^2) < \Theta(n^{\log n})$$

Step 3: Match with the Options

We need an option that lists the functions in this order:

[Functions with $\sqrt{n}$] $\rightarrow$ [$4^{\log n}$] $\rightarrow$ [$2^{\log^2 n}$]

Let's look at Option C:

  1. $5\sqrt{n}$ (Complexity: $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$)

  2. $(\sqrt{2})^{\log n}$ (Complexity: $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$)

  3. $4^{\log n}$ (Complexity: $\Theta(n^2)$)

  4. $2^{\log^2 n}$ (Complexity: $\Theta(n^{\log n})$)

This matches our derived hierarchy. Note that while $5\sqrt{n}$ is technically larger than $\sqrt{n}$ by a constant factor, they belong to the same complexity class, and this is the only option that places the complexity classes in the correct increasing order.

Correct Answer:

C. $5\sqrt{n}, \quad (\sqrt{2})^{\log n}, \quad 4^{\log n}, \quad 2^{\log^2 n}$

questions.qtext:
Consider two programs given below. Consider a non-empty linked list which is either a circular or singly linked list. $\text{P1}$ and $\text{P2}$ are two programs which try to check if it is circular or not. Let $\text{head}$ point to the first node of the linked list.

$\text{P1}$ takes the head of the linked list as its argument and $\text{P2}$ takes head as the first argument and head->next as the second argument at the first call.

int P1(struct node* head)
{
 if (head==null)
 return 1;
 struct node* next = head->next;
 while(next!=null && next !=head)
 next = next->next;
 return (next == head);
}

int P2(struct node* head, struct node* cur)
{
 if (head==null)
 return 1;
 if(cur==null)
 return 0;
 if(head==cur)
 return 1;
 return P2(head, cur->next);
}

Which of the following is/are true?

options.text: $\text{P1}$ returns $1$ if given linked list is circular
$\text{P2}$ returns $1$ if given linked list is circular
$\text{P1}$ returns $1$ if given linked list is having even number of nodes
$\text{P2}$ returns $1$ if given linked list is having even number of nodes

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B

Source solution 1 (score: 6)

Answer to the question is Options : A , B

Option A : If given a circular linked list in P1 at some point of time next will become equal to head and returns head==next i.e,1

Option B : If given a circular linked list in P2 at some point of time cur will become equal to head and returns 1
